title: The Fine Line Between High Engagement and Micromanagement
author: Admired Leadership
summary: This article tackles the tension between staying informed as a leader and slipping into micromanagement. It catalogs the costs of micromanaging, demotivation, bottlenecked progress, and stripped autonomy, then offers a model for staying engaged without overstepping: set clear expectations, flag anticipated obstacles, hand off execution, and check in with two simple questions rather than directing the work. The piece closes with a memorable rule of thumb, 'eyes on, hands off' except when a project genuinely needs rescuing.
points: Micromanagement demotivates team members and turns leaders into productivity bottlenecks.
Engaged leaders set expectations and flag obstacles, then hand off execution to the team.
A simple check-in model: ask 'what should I know?' and 'what can I do to help?' rather than directing.
The rule of thumb offered is 'eyes on, hands off,' reserving 'hands on' for genuine rescue situations.
quotes: Micromanagers monitor even low-priority tasks and assignments and often give frequent feedback about what they believe are the right choices for executing them.
When micromanaged, team members feel undervalued, underappreciated, and suspect in their problem-solving abilities.
Good leaders keep their eyes on and their hands off everything that is going on in the team.
They check in on occasion with two questions: What should I know? And what can I do to help?
Eyes on, Hands off,” unless the project needs to be saved. Then it’s “Hands on” all the way.
